meta.ogDescription: Really Shakespeare — Twelfth Night, Act 3, Scene 3. The twist: the famous triple "thanks" is an editor's repair of a short line in the 1623 First Folio.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Shakespeare: the line is Sebastian’s, spoken to Antonio in Twelfth Night, Act 3, Scene 3, first printed in the 1623 First Folio. One caveat worth knowing — the Folio prints a short line, “thankes; and euer oft,” and the third “thanks” — the one after “and ever” — that makes the famous triple was supplied by a later editor.

source.heading: Sebastian, broke and grateful, in a street in Illyria

docMeta.dd: Twelfth Night, or What You Will — Act 3, Scene 3
c. 1601–1602; first printed in the First Folio, 1623
The Folio reads “thankes; and euer oft”; the third “thanks,” the one after “and ever,” is an editorial completion

source.excerpt:
My kind Antonio,
I can no other answer make but thanks,
And thanks, and ever thanks; and oft good turns
Are shuffled off with such uncurrent pay.
But were my worth, as is my conscience, firm,
You should find better dealing.
trail: The scene is Twelfth Night, Act 3, Scene 3 in the Folger Shakespeare Library edition ↗, where Sebastian answers Antonio: “My kind Antonio, / I can no other answer make but thanks, / And thanks, and ever ⌜thanks; and⌝ oft good turns / Are shuffled off with such uncurrent pay.” The Internet Shakespeare Editions modern text ↗ prints the same reading at 3.3.13–16.

Those half-brackets are explained by the Folger textual notes ↗, whose entry for 3.3.16 reads “thanks, and ever thanks; and oft] Ed.; thankes; and euer oft F.” The same page defines F as the First Folio and “Ed.” as an earlier editor of Shakespeare, beginning with Rowe in 1709.

Freely available older texts still show the unrepaired line: the MIT online Twelfth Night ↗ and the Globe text at the Perseus Digital Library ↗ both give “And thanks; and ever … oft good turns,” with a gap where the third “thanks” is supplied elsewhere.

Wikipedia’s article on the play ↗ dates its composition to around 1601–1602, records the first documented public performance on 2 February 1602 (noted in the diary of the law student John Manningham), and confirms the play was not published until its inclusion in the 1623 First Folio.
source.excerptNote: The text as modern editions print it. In the 1623 First Folio the third line is short — the Folio reads “thankes; and euer oft” — and the Folger edition marks the supplied words in half-brackets to show exactly where the repair falls.

source.rightsNote: Twelfth Night was written around 1601–1602 and first printed in the 1623 First Folio, so the play is centuries into the public domain. The familiar “and ever thanks” reading is an editorial completion that entered the text through the post-1709 editorial tradition — the Folger credits only “Ed.,” which it defines as an editor from Rowe’s 1709 edition onward — so that wording is long out of copyright too. The notes, glosses and layout of any modern edition remain its publisher’s.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare (c. 1564–1616) was an English playwright, poet and actor, and the most quoted writer in the language. Twelfth Night, written around 1601–1602, was never printed in his lifetime: it survives because two of his colleagues in the King’s Men, John Heminges and Henry Condell, gathered his plays into the First Folio of 1623. That single volume is the only authority for every word of this play — and the reason editors have been quietly repairing its damaged verse ever since.

misattribution.heading: The author is right — the wording is part editor
misattribution.intro: This one is not a false credit. Shakespeare wrote the passage and it sits in a play we can point to. What deserves a footnote is the quotation itself: the triple “thanks, and thanks, and ever thanks” is the reading of modern edited texts, not of the only early printing we have.

items.who: An unnamed later editor, not the 1623 Folio
items.why: The Folger edition’s collation for this line reads “thanks, and ever thanks; and oft] Ed.; thankes; and euer oft F” — F being the First Folio, and “Ed.” meaning an earlier editor of Shakespeare, which the same page defines as beginning with Rowe in 1709. The Folio’s reading already contains the second “thanks”; it is the third, after “and ever,” that was added to complete a short line, and no single editor is credited with it: see the Folger textual notes ↗.

items.who: Older public-domain editions, which print less
items.why: Not every free text agrees with the popular quotation. The MIT online Twelfth Night ↗ gives the shorter line, marking a gap where scholarly editions supply the third “thanks,” while Project Gutenberg’s text ↗ prints the fuller emended reading.

items.who: Nobody in particular — the line circulates with no character attached
items.why: The line is usually circulated as a bare Shakespeare thank-you tag, with no play or character attached. It belongs to Sebastian, addressing his rescuer Antonio, in Act 3, Scene 3 ↗.

Stopping at “ever thanks” turns a wry remark into a greeting card. Sebastian’s sentence runs on: “and oft good turns / Are shuffled off with such uncurrent pay” — kindness repaid in worthless coin — as the Internet Shakespeare Editions text ↗ shows.

misattribution.truthLine: Shakespeare wrote it and Sebastian speaks it, in Twelfth Night 3.3 ↗ — but the third “thanks” is an editor’s completion of a line the First Folio prints short ↗.

context.heading: Gratitude as the only currency he has left
lead: Sebastian has just been pulled out of a shipwreck and is being followed around a strange city by the man who saved him. He has no money, no standing and nothing to give back, which is exactly why the speech turns into an accounting metaphor: good turns, he says, get “shuffled off with such uncurrent pay” — settled up in coin that is no longer legal tender. Thanks is the only currency in his pocket, and he knows it is worth less than what he owes.

That is what the internet’s favourite thank-you line is actually about. Quoted alone it reads as warm, uncomplicated gratitude; in the play it opens a rueful thought about how badly kindness tends to get repaid, and Sebastian promises that if his means matched his conscience, Antonio “should find better dealing.”
detailsBody: The passage is also a small lesson in how Shakespeare reaches us. Twelfth Night was never printed while he lived, so the 1623 First Folio is the sole authority for every word of it. At this point the Folio’s verse comes up short, and editors from the eighteenth century onward completed the line by repeating “thanks” — a repair so natural that it became the quotation everyone knows.
